statement: As described second-hand by a narrative review of 14 small laboratory studies (none of the primary studies was read here), people given cocaine with alcohol did not rate themselves as more drunk than with alcohol alone: in three studies cocaine produced a slight decrease in rated drunkenness (the review's table calls the fall non-significant in two of them) and in one it had no effect, while ratings of the cocaine high, or of global intoxication, were greater in six studies when alcohol came before or with the cocaine (in one of the six, the multiple-dose study read in full, the rise in rated any high fell short of significance, p = .09). Cocaine also lessened some alcohol-related deficits on laboratory tests (digit-symbol substitution, sedation, learning and psychomotor tasks), and blood alcohol with cocaine was unchanged in one study and about 10% lower, not significantly, in four. In the multiple-dose study, blood alcohol was lower with cocaine (99 against 118 mg/dL at one time point), no rating of drunkenness was reported, and a rating of feeling sleepy did not differ. The same review reports that 21 of 600 fatally injured drivers in Los Angeles County and 12 of 285 in Spain tested positive for both drugs, which it reads as no definitive protection from the impairing effects of alcohol, and it describes no study that asked other people how drunk someone who had taken both appeared. The laboratory studies had 6 to 34 people each (13 of the 14 had 12 or fewer) and measured self-ratings and task scores in a laboratory; they do not show how drunk someone looks to others or how they would drive.
plain: Can cocaine make someone feel less drunk? In several small laboratory studies, summarized by a review article, people given cocaine with alcohol did not rate themselves as more drunk than with alcohol alone, and some rated themselves slightly less drunk, though the differences were small and mostly not clearly different from chance. Blood alcohol was about the same or a little lower. Cocaine also made some alcohol-related test scores less poor, and people rated the cocaine high stronger when alcohol came first. None of these studies shows how drunk someone looks to other people, and records of drivers who died show that some had both drugs in their blood, so the combination did not clearly protect them from alcohol's effects. This rests on a review of other people's work, not on the original studies, so it is a first outline.
population: Adults in prospective laboratory studies of alcohol with cocaine, 6 to 34 people each (13 of 14 studies with 12 or fewer), as described in one narrative review; fatally injured drivers in Los Angeles County (600) and Spain (285)
exposure: Cocaine (taken by the nose or injected, never smoked) with alcohol, mostly given before or with the cocaine, in doses set by the researchers and listed in the review's Table 1; study conditions only
comparator: The same people given alcohol alone (laboratory studies); drivers who died with alcohol alone (retrospective records)
outcome: Self-rated drunkenness (inebriation) and rated high, scores on tests of learning and movement, blood alcohol, and the presence of both drugs in fatally injured drivers
magnitude: No effect size is reported for rated drunkenness. Pennings et al. (2002), second-hand: slight decrease in rated drunkenness with cocaine in three studies (Farre 1993, 9 people; Higgins 1993, 8; Farre 1997, 8; Table 1 labels the Farre falls non-significant) and no effect in one (Perez-Reyes and Jeffcoat 1992, 11); rated cocaine high or global intoxication greater with alcohol before or with cocaine in six studies (the review's list includes McCance-Katz et al. 1998, in which any high was short of significance, p = .09); blood alcohol unchanged in one study and about 10% lower, non-significantly, in four; alcohol-induced deficits lessened by cocaine in digit-symbol substitution, sedation, and learning and psychomotor performance; 21 of 600 fatally injured drivers in Los Angeles County and 12 of 285 in Spain positive for both drugs. McCance-Katz et al. (1998): plasma alcohol 99 (SE 7) against 118 (10) mg/dL 90 minutes into the session, p = .008; no drunkenness rating reported.

evidence.locator: Results > Prospective research > Effect on perceived inebriation, 1st paragraph (pp. 776-777); Table 1 (p. 775)
evidence.extracted: As described by the review: in several studies cocaine produced a slight decrease in alcohol-induced inebriation (Farre 1993; Higgins 1993; Farre 1997) and in another it had no effect (Perez-Reyes and Jeffcoat 1992); Table 1 labels the Farre studies' falls non-significantly reduced drunk and lists 9, 8, 8 and 11 people in the four studies. Alcohol given before or together with cocaine led to a greater perceived cocaine high or global intoxication in six studies; an EEG index of intoxication rose in step with the high in one; alcohol raised the preference for cocaine over cash in one.

As described by the review: alcohol-induced deficits in the laboratory were consistently lessened by cocaine: digit-symbol substitution (Foltin 1993; Higgins 1993), sedation (Foltin 1993), and learning and psychomotor performance (Higgins 1992).

evidence.locator: Results > Prospective research > Blood levels and toxicokinetics, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: As described by the review: compared with alcohol alone, the combination had no effect on blood alcohol in one study and produced a slight, non-significant decrease (about 10%) in four. The review offers reduced alcohol absorption after cocaine narrows blood vessels as one possible explanation and says cocaethylene is too small to account for the lower alcohol levels.

evidence.locator: Retrospective studies > Operating motor vehicles, 1st paragraph (p. 778); Conclusions, 2nd paragraph (starts p. 780; the driving sentence is on p. 781)
evidence.extracted: As described by the review: retrospective research shows a substantial effect of alcohol alone on driving, and the combination gave no definitive protection from alcohol's impairing effects, since 21 of 600 fatally injured drivers in Los Angeles County and 12 of 285 in Spain tested positive for both drugs; the conclusions say there is no evidence that co-use of cocaine adds to alcohol-induced driving deficits. The abstract's statement that cocaine counters driving deficits has no prospective driving test behind it in the text.

evidence.locator: Methods and Materials > Cocaine Study Drug Administration Sessions, 1st paragraph (pp. 251-252); Results, 2nd, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (pp. 252-253); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (pp. 255-256)
evidence.extracted: The one multiple-dose study read in full reports visual analogue ratings of any high, rush, sleepy, paranoid, sad or depressed, crash, desire for cocaine and feel good, and a quality-of-high scale, but no rating of drunkenness or intoxication; sleepy showed no significant difference between conditions (no values printed), and any high was higher with the combination than with cocaine alone but short of significance (p = .09), although the review counts this study among six with a greater high. Plasma alcohol was lower with cocaine than with alcohol alone (p = .008; 99 against 118 mg/dL 90 minutes into the session).

risk_of_bias.note: The primary studies cannot be appraised from the review: it gives no study-level risk-of-bias assessment, and its tables disagree with its text in places (card reporting issues).

inconsistency.note: Three studies found a slight fall in rated drunkenness and one found no effect; none found a rise.

indirectness.note: Second-hand through a narrative review, and based on self-rated drunkenness and test scores in a laboratory, not on how drunk someone appears to others or on real-world impairment.

imprecision.note: Studies of 8 to 11 people; the review's table labels the falls non-significant, and no effect sizes are given.

grade.reasoning: A claim seen only through a review starts from the design of the primary studies it describes (placebo-controlled, blind crossover laboratory studies, which start high) and is downgraded for risk of bias, because they cannot be appraised from the review (-1), for indirectness, because the findings are second-hand self-ratings and test scores in a laboratory (-1), and for imprecision, because the studies are small and the review's table labels the fall in rated drunkenness non-significant (-1). Certainty very low. Because every supporting anchor is a narrative review, the claim stays at draft and says so in its statement (METHODS 6.3). Status: single study (one review; its studies were not read). The roadside-fatality figures are context: they show that people who had taken both drugs were not protected from alcohol's effects, not whether they looked less drunk.

verification.flag_note: Rests on Pennings et al. (2002) as described; none of the primary studies (Farre 1993 and 1997, Higgins 1993, Perez-Reyes and Jeffcoat 1992, Foltin 1993, Higgins 1992) was read and none has a reference record here, so the claim stays at draft. WRITING-RULES rule 0: the practical worry is that a person who feels less drunk, or is thought sober by others, takes on more risk; the sources measure only self-ratings and test scores, and no source asks other people to judge how drunk someone looks. McCance-Katz et al. (1998) is used as a qualifier only (no drunkenness rating was reported). The study cards sc_pennings_2002 and sc_mccance_katz_1998 are staged in data/study-cards/_incoming/interactions/ and must be merged first.
